Field-based studies of the Greater sooty owl (Tyto tenebricosa) indicate that hatchlings emerge from eggs incubated at 33 °C [T = 33 °C] after a developmental period of 42 days [ab = 42 days], a duration that aligns with the prolonged incubation typical of large, forest-dwelling strigiforms. Upon hatching, these altricial nestlings exhibit a remarkably modest neonatal body mass of 42.5 grams [Ww0 = 42.5 grams], a value that underscores the considerable energetic investment required to attain the substantial adult dimensions characteristic of this species. This initial weight is followed by a sustained phase of rapid mass gain, fueled by intensive biparental provisioning of small mammals and birds within the dense temperate rainforests of southeastern Australia. The nestling period culminates in a critical developmental milestone: under the thermoneutral conditions typical of the species' active metabolic phase (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), fledging, defined by the achievement of sustained flight, occurs at 84 days after hatching [tx = 84 days after hatching], marking the transition to a dispersive juvenile stage.

Following the fledging event, immature individuals enter a protracted juvenile phase characterized by continued somatic growth and the gradual refinement of hunting skills. The period between fledging and the attainment of reproductive competence is substantial, with puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation, estimated to occur at 252 days after hatching [tp = 252 days after hatching] when maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively delayed sexual maturation, compared to smaller Tyto species, is likely a consequence of the energy demands required to reach the species' considerable adult body size. Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism: females, the larger sex, attain an ultimate wet weight of 887 grams [Wwi = 887 grams], while males reach a substantially lower final mass of 492 grams [Wwi = 492 grams]. This dimorphism, with females being roughly 1.8 times heavier than males, is among the most extreme recorded in the genus Tyto and is thought to facilitate the female's role in extended incubation and brood defense.

Reproductive output in the Greater sooty owl is constrained by the seasonal availability of prey in its cool, mesic forest habitat. Females typically produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], and within that reproductive event, they lay a clutch of two eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of two eggs]. This low annual fecundity, representing the maximum reproductive rate for the species, is a life-history strategy characteristic of long-lived, K-selected avian predators that invest heavily in a small number of high-quality offspring. The first successful breeding event is deferred until well after the juvenile dispersal phase, with the time since birth at first brood recorded at approximately 548 days [tR = approximately 548 days] under standard thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This extended period to first reproduction, relative to smaller owls, reflects the time necessary for young birds to establish a territory and acquire the hunting proficiency required to provision a nest successfully.

Metabolic physiology in this species reflects its adaptation to a relatively cool, low-energy environment. Respirometry trials conducted on resting adults under post-absorptive conditions at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] have measured a basal oxygen consumption of 518 milliliters per hour [JOi = 518 milliliters per hour]. This basal metabolic rate aligns closely with allometric predictions for a 492-gram male or an 887-gram female, but is notably low compared to active metabolic rates observed during flight or territorial calling. The species also exhibits exceptional longevity for an owl of its body size; the maximum lifespan recorded in the wild, again at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is approximately 23 years [am = approximately 23 years]. Such extended survival, coupled with low annual reproductive output, suggests a life-history strategy heavily reliant on high adult survivorship and stable, low-mortality environments.

Comparative analyses within the Tytonidae reveal that the Greater sooty owl's life-history parameters are consistent with a slow pace-of-life syndrome. The combination of a moderate neonatal mass of 42.5 grams [Ww0 = 42.5 grams] and an exceptionally long developmental period to fledging at 84 days [tx = 84 days] is unusual among owls, even when accounting for its large ultimate body size. at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]The substantial difference between the female ultimate wet weight of 887 grams [Wwi = 887 grams] and the male value of 492 grams [Wwi = 492 grams] highlights a reproductive strategy where females bear the energetic costs of egg production and extended incubation. Furthermore, the deferred age at first breeding—quantified as approximately 548 days since birth [tR = approximately 548 days since birth] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]—coupled with a maximum reproductive rate of just two eggs per year (a single clutch produced annually [F_R_i = a single clutch produced annually], containing two eggs [N_R_i = containing two eggs]) reinforces the profile of a species that prioritizes individual survival and territory occupancy over iteroparous, high-fecundity reproduction.
